subject: Copywriting
title: The Tabloid Formula
description: A fast breakdown of The Tabloid Formula for builders.

hook.text: British tabloids perfected headline writing. The Sun's 'GOTCHA!' after sinking an Argentine ship sold millions.

buildup.text: Tabloid rules: short words, active verbs, emotional triggers. 'SLAMS,' 'FURY,' 'SHOCK'—each one a punch.

discovery.text: The alliteration trick: 'Super Saturday Scorcher.' Sound patterns make headlines sticky and fun to say aloud.

twist.text: Tabloid headlines distort as much as they inform. Studies show they shape opinions more than the articles.

climax.text: Online clickbait borrowed every tabloid technique, just digitized. The Sun invented BuzzFeed's playbook.

punchline.text: Tabloids wrote the rules. The internet just copied them.

quiz.question: Which technique makes tabloid headlines memorable?
options: Short words, active verbs, and alliteration

details.summary: Tabloid headlines follow a formula: short words, present tense, emotional punch, and often alliteration. The British tabloid tradition — 'Gotcha!' (The Sun on the Falklands), 'It's The Sun Wot Won It' — perfected the art of compressing complex stories into scannable, emotionally charged phrases.
details.whyItMatters: Tabloid headlines are the most disciplined headline writing in journalism. Their ruthless economy of language offers lessons for anyone writing in attention-scarce environments.
takeaways: Tabloids use short words, present tense, and emotional compression
Alliteration and wordplay increase memorability and shareability
The best tabloid headlines tell the story in fewer than ten words

faq.question: What makes tabloid headlines different from broadsheet headlines?
faq.answer: Tabloids prioritize emotional impact and brevity. Broadsheets prioritize factual accuracy and context. A broadsheet might write 'Prime Minister Resigns Amid Scandal.' A tabloid would write 'PM QUITS!' The tabloid sacrifices nuance for punch — a deliberate editorial choice.

faq.question: Can tabloid headline techniques be used in marketing?
faq.answer: Yes — their principles of brevity, emotion, and concrete language apply broadly. Subject lines, social posts, and ad copy all benefit from tabloid discipline. The tabloid forces writers to find the single most powerful way to express an idea.
